title: Philippe Schwaller
text:
Philippe Schwaller joined EPFL as a tenure-track assistant professor in the Institute of Chemical Sciences and Engineering in February 2022. He leads the Laboratory of Artificial Chemical Intelligence, which works on AI-accelerated discovery and synthesis of molecules and materials. Philippe is also a core PI of NCCR Catalysis.
His research focuses on chemical reasoning, reaction prediction, synthesis planning, generative molecular design, and adaptive experimentation.



Five years at IBM Research Zürich with Dr. Teodoro Laino
PhD in Chemistry and Molecular Sciences, University of Bern, 2021, with Prof. Jean-Louis Reymond
MPhil in Physics, University of Cambridge, 2019
BSc and MSc in Materials Science and Engineering, EPFL, 2014 and 2016

title: Research
text:
At LIAC, we develop artificial intelligence and machine-learning methods for chemical reasoning, synthesis planning, molecular and materials discovery, and experimental optimization. We aim to connect predictive models to the decisions that chemists make and, ultimately, to experiments that generate new knowledge.
Our main research directions include:

title: Research
text:
Selected Research Highlights








Synthegy: strategy-aware chemical reasoning



Matter, 2026. Large language models guide chemical search algorithms using strategies written in natural language, enabling steerable retrosynthesis and reaction-mechanism elucidation.
Paper · Preprint










Sample-efficient generative molecular design using memory manipulation



Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026. Saturn combines the Mamba architecture with augmented memory to learn more from each scored molecule and directly optimize high-fidelity objectives.
Paper · Code










TANGO: direct optimization of constrained synthesizability



Nature Computational Science, 2026. TANGO guides generative models toward molecules that use required starting materials or intermediates, making synthesizability part of the design objective.
Paper










Swarm intelligence for chemical-reaction optimization



Chem, 2026. α-PSO combines interpretable particle-swarm dynamics with machine-learning guidance for parallel experimental optimization.
Paper · Code










Highly parallel optimization of chemical reactions



Nature Communications, 2025. Minerva couples Bayesian optimization with automated 96-well experimentation to navigate large reaction-condition spaces.
Paper · Code










A multi-modal transformer for predicting global minimum adsorption energy



Nature Communications, 2025. AdsMT predicts global minimum adsorption energies without enumerating binding sites and uses cross-attention to identify favorable adsorption locations.
Paper










Data-driven synthesis predictions of colloidal nanocrystal shapes



Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2025. Machine learning, electronic-lab-notebook data, Bayesian optimization, and experiments were combined to navigate copper-nanocrystal synthesis.
Paper










ChemCrow: augmenting large-language models with chemistry tools



Nature Machine Intelligence, 2024. ChemCrow demonstrated how a language model can plan and execute complex chemistry tasks by using purpose-built tools.
Paper · Code

title: Schwaller Group at EPFL
text:
The Laboratory of Artificial Chemical Intelligence (LIAC) is part of the Institute of Chemical Sciences and Engineering at École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Switzerland. The lab is led by Prof. Philippe Schwaller.
At LIAC, we develop artificial intelligence and machine-learning methods for chemical reasoning, synthesis planning, molecular and materials discovery, and experimental optimization. We pursue fundamental science driven by real-world applications, with a particular focus on sustainability.
LIAC is derived from the French laboratory name, Laboratoire d’intelligence artificielle en chimie.

title: Schwaller Group at EPFL
text:
Recent research highlights

Synthegy combines large language models with chemical search tools for strategy-aware synthesis planning and reaction-mechanism elucidation. Matter (2026)
Saturn and TANGO make generative molecular design more sample-efficient and directly optimize for synthesizability. Saturn · TANGO
α-PSO uses interpretable swarm intelligence and machine learning for parallel chemical-reaction optimization. Chem (2026)

See more research highlights.

title: Openings
text:
Are you excited about machine learning applied to chemical sciences? LIAC brings together chemistry, computer science, materials science, and experimental research.
Last reviewed: August 2026.

title: Openings
text:
Postdoctoral Position
We have one two-year postdoctoral position on advancing strategic synthesis planning with machine learning and large language models. The project builds on our recent work in strategy-aware chemical reasoning and tool-augmented chemistry agents.
The 2026 EPFL postdoctoral starting salary is CHF 88,000 gross per year, including the 13th salary month. See the official EPFL salary scale for details.
If you are interested, fill in the following form:
Apply for the postdoctoral position

title: Openings
text:
PhD Positions
There are no immediate PhD openings. New funded positions will be posted here. Information about admission is available from the EPFL doctoral program in chemistry and chemical engineering.

title: Openings
text:
Master’s Theses and Semester Projects
We regularly supervise projects for students interested in applying machine learning to chemical science. Depending on the project, you might work on chemical data, molecular representations, synthesis planning, generative models, scientific language models, or experimental optimization.
Please contact Prof. Philippe Schwaller with a short description of your interests, your CV and transcript, your availability, and a link to previous technical work if available.

title: Openings
text:
Postdoctoral Fellowships
We are happy to discuss strong fellowship proposals that fit LIAC’s research directions. Relevant programs include the EPFL AI Center and Swiss AI Initiative Postdoctoral Fellowships.
We strongly encourage applications from people with different backgrounds, identities, disciplines, and career paths. Every new colleague brings a different perspective, and we see that diversity as part of doing better science.
